title: UNIT 3: EXPONENTIAL AND LOGARITHMIC FUNCTIONS
notes:
Exponent → tells how many times a base is used as a factor.

Example: 2⁵ = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32.

Base → the number being raised to a power.
Exponent → the power to which the base is raised.

Note: (−3)² = 9, but −3² = −9.

Laws of Exponents:
✓ aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ
✓ aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ, a ≠ 0
✓ (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ
✓ (ab)ⁿ = aⁿbⁿ
✓ (a/b)ⁿ = aⁿ/bⁿ, b ≠ 0

Zero exponent → a⁰ = 1, a ≠ 0.

Negative exponent → a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ.

Rational exponent → a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a.

General form → a^(m/n) = ⁿ√(aᵐ) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ.

If n is even and a < 0, a^(1/n) is not a real number. If n is odd, it can be real.

Irrational exponents → expressions such as 3^√2; the laws of exponents continue to apply.

title: LOGARITHMS
notes:
Logarithm → the exponent to which a base must be raised to obtain a given positive number.

Definition:
logₐ c = b ⇔ aᵇ = c
where a > 0, a ≠ 1 and c > 0.

Example:
log₂ 8 = 3 because 2³ = 8.

Conversion:
Exponential → 2⁵ = 32
Logarithmic → log₂ 32 = 5.

Important values:
✓ logₐ 1 = 0
✓ logₐ a = 1
✓ logₐ(aᵖ) = p
✓ a^(logₐ p) = p

Laws of Logarithms:
✓ logₐ(MN) = logₐM + logₐN
✓ logₐ(M/N) = logₐM − logₐN
✓ logₐ(Mʳ) = r logₐM

Logarithms are defined only when the argument is positive.

Example:
log₃(1/9) = −2 because 3⁻² = 1/9.

title: COMMON LOGARITHMS & ANTILOGARITHMS
notes:
Common logarithm → logarithm with base 10.

log₁₀M is usually written simply as log M.

Examples:
✓ log 10 = 1
✓ log 100 = 2
✓ log 1000 = 3
✓ log 0.1 = −1
✓ log 0.01 = −2

Characteristic + Mantissa:
For a positive number written as M = m × 10ᶜ,
log M = log m + c.

Characteristic → integer part.
Mantissa → fractional part.

Example:
345 = 3.45 × 10²
Therefore, log 345 = log 3.45 + 2.

Antilogarithm → the inverse operation of logarithm.
If log M = N, then M = antilog(N).

Important:
antilog(log M) = M.

Logarithms can also be used to approximate complicated calculations involving multiplication, division, powers and roots.

title: CHANGE OF BASE FORMULA
notes:
Change of Base:

logₐM = log_bM / log_ba

where a > 0, b > 0, a ≠ 1 and b ≠ 1.

This allows a logarithm to be evaluated using another convenient base, such as 10 or e.

Example:
log₂5 = log 5 / log 2.

Important warning:
◆ logₐ(MN) ≠ (logₐM)(logₐN)
◆ logₐ(M + N) ≠ logₐM + logₐN
◆ logₐ(M/N) ≠ (logₐM)/(logₐN).

title: EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS
notes:
Exponential function:
f(x) = aˣ
where a > 0, a ≠ 1 and x is any real number.

Domain → ℝ (all real numbers).
Range → positive real numbers (0, ∞).
y-intercept → (0, 1).
x-intercept → none.
Horizontal asymptote → y = 0.

If a > 1:
✓ Function is increasing.
✓ Values grow rapidly as x increases.
✓ Values approach 0 as x becomes very negative.

If 0 < a < 1:
✓ Function is decreasing.
✓ Values decrease as x increases.
✓ Values approach 0 as x becomes very positive.

Example:
f(x) = 2ˣ
f(−1) = 1/2
f(0) = 1
f(1) = 2
f(2) = 4.

Exponential functions can model rapid growth and decline, such as population growth and decay.

title: EXPONENTIAL GRAPHS
notes:
For y = aˣ, a > 1:
The graph rises from left to right and approaches the x-axis without touching it.

For y = aˣ, 0 < a < 1:
The graph falls from left to right and approaches the x-axis without touching it.

Both types:
✓ Pass through (0, 1).
✓ Have domain ℝ.
✓ Have range (0, ∞).
✓ Have horizontal asymptote y = 0.
✓ Have no x-intercept.

Negative exponential:
y = −eˣ
has domain ℝ, range of negative real numbers, y-intercept (0, −1), and horizontal asymptote y = 0.

title: NATURAL EXPONENTIAL FUNCTION
notes:
The number e is an important mathematical constant.

e ≈ 2.71828.

Natural exponential function:
f(x) = eˣ.

e is defined as the value approached by (1 + 1/n)ⁿ as n becomes very large.

Examples:
e² ≈ 7.38906
e⁻¹ ≈ 0.36788
e³·⁵ ≈ 33.11545.

The natural exponential function is widely used in growth, decay and other mathematical applications.

title: LOGARITHMIC FUNCTIONS
notes:
Logarithmic function:
f(x) = logₐx
where a > 0 and a ≠ 1.

Domain → (0, ∞).
Range → ℝ.
x-intercept → (1, 0).
y-intercept → none.
Vertical asymptote → x = 0.

If a > 1:
✓ Function is increasing.
✓ f(x) increases as x increases.

If 0 < a < 1:
✓ Function is decreasing.
✓ f(x) decreases as x increases.

Example:
log₂1 = 0
log₂2 = 1
log₂4 = 2
log₂8 = 3.

x must always be positive for logₐx.

title: TRANSFORMATIONS OF LOGARITHMIC GRAPHS
notes:
For f(x) = logₐx:

−f(x) → reflection of the graph in the x-axis.

f(−x) → reflection of the graph in the y-axis.

Example:
g(x) = −log₂x
is the reflection of y = log₂x across the x-axis.

h(x) = log₂(−x)
is the reflection of y = log₂x across the y-axis.

title: NATURAL LOGARITHM
notes:
Natural logarithm → logarithm with base e.

ln x = logₑx.

Important values:
✓ ln 1 = 0
✓ ln e = 1
✓ ln(eˣ) = x
✓ e^(ln x) = x

Examples:
ln(e³) = 3
ln(1/e) = −1.

The graphs y = eˣ and y = ln x are inverse functions and are reflections of each other across the line y = x.

title: SOLVING EXPONENTIAL EQUATIONS
notes:
Exponential equation → an equation in which the variable occurs in an exponent.

Method 1 → Express both sides using the same base.

Example:
2^(2x−1) = 8
2^(2x−1) = 2³
2x − 1 = 3
x = 2.

Base-exponent property:
aˣ = aʸ ⇔ x = y
for a > 0 and a ≠ 1.

Method 2 → Use logarithms when the bases cannot easily be made equal.

Steps:
✓ Isolate the exponential expression.
✓ Take logarithms of both sides.
✓ Use the power law to bring the exponent down.
✓ Solve for the variable.

Example:
2ˣ = 20
x = log 20 / log 2 ≈ 4.32226.

title: SOLVING LOGARITHMIC EQUATIONS
notes:
Logarithmic equation → an equation containing the logarithm of an expression involving a variable.

First state the universe/domain by requiring every logarithm argument to be positive.

Steps:
✓ State the universe.
✓ Collect logarithmic terms.
✓ Convert to exponential form or use logarithm laws.
✓ Solve for the variable.
✓ Check that the solution satisfies the logarithm restrictions.

Example:
log₂(x + 3) = 4
x + 3 = 2⁴
x + 3 = 16
x = 13.

Since x + 3 > 0, x > −3; therefore x = 13 is valid.

title: RELATION BETWEEN EXPONENTIAL & LOGARITHMIC FUNCTIONS
notes:
Exponential and logarithmic functions with the same base are inverses.

If:
y = aˣ
then:
y = logₐx.

Inverse relationships:
✓ a^(logₐx) = x
✓ logₐ(aˣ) = x.

Their graphs are reflections of each other across the line y = x.

Domain of y = aˣ = Range of y = logₐx.
Range of y = aˣ = Domain of y = logₐx.

For y = aˣ:
Domain = ℝ
Range = (0, ∞)

For y = logₐx:
Domain = (0, ∞)
Range = ℝ.

Exponential y-intercept → (0, 1).
Logarithmic x-intercept → (1, 0).

Exponential horizontal asymptote → y = 0.
Logarithmic vertical asymptote → x = 0.

title: APPLICATION: COMPOUND INTEREST
notes:
Compound interest → interest that is added to the principal so that future interest is calculated on the increased amount.

If compounded once per year:
A(t) = P(1 + r)ᵗ.

If compounded n times per year:
A(t) = P(1 + r/n)ⁿᵗ.

Where:
P → principal amount
r → annual interest rate as a decimal
n → number of compounding periods per year
t → number of years
A(t) → amount after t years.

Example:
If Birr 20,000 is invested at 7% annually for 5 years:
A = 20,000(1.07)⁵
≈ Birr 28,051.03.

More frequent compounding generally produces a larger amount for the same nominal annual rate and time.

title: UNIT 3 QUICK REVIEW
notes:
Exponent → indicates repeated multiplication.

Main exponent laws:
✓ aᵐaⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ
✓ (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ
✓ a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ
✓ aᵐ/aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ
✓ aᵐ⁄ⁿ = ⁿ√(aᵐ).

Logarithm → an exponent.
logₐx = y ⇔ aʸ = x.

Main logarithm laws:
✓ logₐ(MN) = logₐM + logₐN
✓ logₐ(M/N) = logₐM − logₐN
✓ logₐ(Mʳ) = rlogₐM.

Exponential: y = aˣ
Domain ℝ, Range (0,∞), asymptote y = 0.

Logarithmic: y = logₐx
Domain (0,∞), Range ℝ, asymptote x = 0.

Exponential and logarithmic functions are inverses.

Exponential functions are used in applications such as compound interest, growth and decay.
